elements.quote: Adolescence and childhood are critical periods for the development of metabolic health, 1 as there are times when changes in diet and lifestyle can have long-term effects on health outcomes. Poor metabolic health in adolescence can lead to the development of chronic diseases such as type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity in adulthood. The prevalence of metabolic disorders is increasing globally, especially among adolescents, and this has become a public health concern. The main features of metabolic health include ideal levels of blood sugar, triglycerides, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, blood pressure and waist circumference. Abnormalities in these metabolic health levels can lead to obesity, hypertension, hyperlipidaemia and insulin resistance. The key contributing factors include diet and behaviour, such as an increased intake of foods containing high amounts of saturated fat and carbohydrates, particularly sweetened beverages; a lack of physical activity; and smoking. The World Health Organization (WHO) recognises the significant impact of diet on disease risk and has developed a Global Action Plan to address unhealthy dietary patterns. The plan aims to reduce behavioural risk factors such as physical inactivity, tobacco use, harmful alcohol consumption and unhealthy eating habits. The WHO recommends various dietary changes to promote better health, including maintaining balanced energy intake, limiting saturated and trans fats, transitioning to unsaturated fats, increasing fruit and vegetable intake, and reducing sugar and salt consumption. These recommendations are often found in regional diets, such as the Mediterranean diet (MedDiet), which is characterised by high consumption of fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, nuts, fish, and olive oil and low consumption of red and processed meats, sweets and refined grains. A MedDiet has been associated with improved metabolic syndrome (MetS) outcomes, including a decreased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and obesity, among adults. Several studies have associated the MedDiet with individual MetS-related factors (blood sugar, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, blood pressure and waist circumference). A recent meta-analysis highlighted that interventions based on a MedDiet are highly effective in lowering childhood and adolescent obesity and body mass index.

Some studies have shown a positive association between adherence to the MedDiet and improved MetS risk, whereas others have reported no significant association. To our knowledge, no previous systematic review or meta-analysis has synthesised the available evidence examining the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents. Therefore, the aim of this systematic review and meta-analysis was to investigate whether adherence to a MedDiet is associated with MetS in this population.

Moreover, our study did not reveal any publication bias. These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al, our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well-designed systematic review and meta-analysis of paediatric populations.
